Understanding (the measure of) Partha's devotion, Durga who is always graciously inclined towards mankind, appeared in the firmament and in the presence of Govinda, said these words. The goddess said,--'Within a short time thou shalt conquer thy foes, O Pandava. O invincible one, thou hast Narayana (again) for aiding thee.'

events.working_title: Krishna Places the Chariot Between the Armies
events.one_line_summary: At Arjuna's request Krishna drives the chariot between the two assembled armies so Arjuna can survey the kinsmen he must fight.

sources.source_excerpt: Arjuna said,--'O thou that knoweth no deterioration, place my car (once) between the two armies, so that I may observe these that stand here desirous of battle...' Sanjaya continued,--'Thus addressed by Gudakesa, O Bharata, Hrishikesa, placing that excellent car between the two armies, in view of Bhishma and Drona and all the kings of the earth, said,--'Behold, O Partha these assembled Kurus.'

events.working_title: Arjuna's Despair and Collapse
events.one_line_summary: Seeing his kinsmen arrayed on both sides, Arjuna is overcome with pity, his bow Gandiva slips from his hand, and he casts aside his weapons and sinks down on his chariot.

sources.source_excerpt: Beholding all those kinsmen standing (there), the son of Kunti, possessed by excessive pity, despondingly said... 'My body trembles, and my hair stands on end. Gandiva slips from my hand, and my skin burns... I wish not to slay these though they slay me, O slayer of Madhu...' Having spoken thus on the field of battle, Arjuna, his mind troubled with grief, casting aside his bow and arrows, sat down on his car.

events.working_title: Arjuna Surrenders to Krishna as Disciple
events.one_line_summary: Unable to see his duty, Arjuna lays down his arms in spirit and begs Krishna to instruct him as his disciple.

sources.source_excerpt: Arjuna said,--'...My nature affected by the taint of compassion, my mind unsettled about (my) duty, I ask thee. Tell me what is assuredly good (for me). I am thy disciple. O, instruct me, I seek thy aid.'

events.working_title: Krishna Grants Celestial Sight and Reveals the Vishvarupa
events.one_line_summary: At Arjuna's request, Krishna gives him divine sight and reveals his supreme universal form filling the heavens.

sources.source_excerpt: Arjuna said,--'...I desire to behold thy sovereign form. If, O Lord, thou thinkest that I am competent to behold that (form), then... show me thy eternal Self.' The Holy One said,--'...Thou art, however, not competent to behold me with this eye of thine. I give thee celestial sight. Behold my sovereign mystic nature.' Sanjaya continued,--'Having said this... Hari, the mighty Lord of mystic power, then revealed to the son of Pritha his Supreme sovereign form, with many mouths and eyes, many wonderous aspects...'

events.working_title: Krishna Declares 'I Am Death'
events.one_line_summary: Within the cosmic form Arjuna sees the warriors rushing into Krishna's flaming mouths, and Krishna reveals himself as all-consuming Time commanding Arjuna to be his instrument.

sources.source_excerpt: Arjuna said,--'...all these sons of Dhritarashtra... are quickly entering thy terrible mouths rendered fierce by thy tusks. Some, with their heads crushed, are seen striking at the interstices of (thy) teeth...' The Holy One said, 'I am Death, the destroyer of the worlds, fully developed. I am now engaged in slaying the race of men... By me have all these been already slain. Be only (my) instrument.'

events.working_title: Krishna Returns to His Gentle Form
events.one_line_summary: Terrified and repentant, Arjuna begs Krishna to resume his familiar form; Krishna comforts him and restores him to his senses.

sources.source_excerpt: Arjuna said,--'...Beholding (thy) form (unseen) before, I have been joyful, (yet) my mind hath been troubled, with fear. Show me that (other ordinary) form, O God...' Sanjaya continued,--'Vasudeva, having said all this to Arjuna, once more showed (him) his own (ordinary) form, and that High-Souled one, assuming once more (his) gentle form, comforted him who had been afflicted.' Arjuna said,--'Beholding this gentle human form of thine, O Janardana, I have now become of right mind and have come to my normal state.'

events.working_title: Arjuna Resolves to Fight
events.one_line_summary: His delusion dispelled, Arjuna declares he will do Krishna's bidding and returns to battle.

sources.source_excerpt: Arjuna said, 'My delusion hath been destroyed, and the recollection (of what I am) hath been gained by me, O Undeteriorating one, through thy favour. I am now firm. My doubts have been dispelled. I will do thy bidding.'

events.working_title: Krishna's Overture to Karna
events.one_line_summary: After the Gita, Krishna approaches Karna and invites him to fight for the Pandavas until Bhishma falls, but Karna refuses out of loyalty to Duryodhana.

sources.source_excerpt: Vasudeva then went to Radha's son on the field of battle. And the elder brother of Gada, for the sake of the Pandavas, then said to Karna,--'It hath been heard by me, O Karna, that from hatred of Bhishma thou wilt not fight. Come to our side, O son of Radha, and (stay with us) as long as Bhishma is not slain...' Karna said, 'I will not do anything that is disagreeable to Dhritarashtra's son, O Kesava. Devoted to Duryodhana's good, know that I have cast off my life (for him).'

events.variant_notes: cf. mb_b_032 (pre-war offer to Karna).

events.working_title: Krishna Counsels Arjuna to Let Karna Pass
events.one_line_summary: Krishna holds Arjuna back from fighting Karna, warning that Karna still holds the infallible dart that Vasava (Indra) gave him.

sources.source_excerpt: Thus addressed by Savyasachin, the mighty-armed Kesava, endued with great energy, replied in these opportune words, 'The mighty-armed Satyaki is singly a match for Karna, O son of Pandu!... For the present, O Partha, it is not proper for thee to fight with Karna. The latter hath with him the blazing dart, like a fierce meteor, that Vasava gave him. O slayer of hostile heroes, he hath kept it for thy sake, worshipping it with reverence... I know, O son of Kunti, this wicked wight's hour, when, indeed, thou wilt, with keen shafts, throw him down from his car.'

events.working_title: Krishna Lends His Car to Satyaki
events.one_line_summary: Krishna foresees Satyaki's need, summons his charioteer Daruka by blowing his conch, and lends his own celestial car to Satyaki for the fight with Karna.

sources.source_excerpt: Before even the encounter, Krishna knew it in his heart that the heroic Satyaki would be vanquished... Janardana, O king, knoweth both the past and the future. For this, summoning his charioteer, Daruka, he had commanded him, saying, 'Let my car be kept equipped tomorrow.' ... With Kesava's permission, upon that car guided by Daruka, and which resembled the blazing fire or the sun in effulgence, ascended the grandson of Sini.

events.working_title: Krishna Embraces and Praises Arjuna After the Vow
events.one_line_summary: When Arjuna's vow against Jayadratha is fulfilled, Krishna embraces him, and Arjuna credits the victory entirely to Krishna's grace.

sources.source_excerpt: At that frightful time when confusion was everywhere... Hrishikesa, stationed in the van of battle embracing Arjuna who had accomplished his vow, told him these words, 'By good luck, O Jishnu, thy great vow hath been accomplished...' Unto him Arjuna replied, 'Through thy grace, O Madhava, this vow that even the gods could with difficulty accomplish, hath been accomplished by me... This is thy victory, O lord!'

events.working_title: Krishna Shows Arjuna the Slain Battlefield
events.one_line_summary: As they ride back across the field, Krishna points out to Arjuna the fallen kings, elephants, and horses slain by his shafts.

sources.source_excerpt: Then Krishna said, 'Desirous of victory in battle or world-wide fame many heroic kings are lying on the earth, struck with thy shafts... Behold, O hero, those huge creatures afflicted with shafts lying on the ground in convulsions... This fame-enhancing and mighty feat on the field of battle is capable of being achieved by thee only, O puissant one...'

events.working_title: Krishna Rallies the Broken Pandava Host
events.one_line_summary: Seeing the Panchalas routed by Drona and Karna, Krishna urges Arjuna to cast away fear and advance against the two great warriors.

sources.source_excerpt: Seeing the Panchalas slaughtered and routed, Janardana becoming cheerless, said these words unto Phalguna, '...Beholding the host fly away, through fear, ye Pandava warriors, cast away your fears! Accompanied by all the forces and arraying then, in good order, both of us, with uplifted weapons, are even now proceeding against Drona and the Suta's son for withstanding them.'

events.working_title: Krishna Sends Ghatotkacha Against Karna
events.one_line_summary: Krishna keeps Arjuna from Karna and instead commands the Rakshasa Ghatotkacha to fight Karna at night, so that Karna's infallible dart is spent on him.

sources.source_excerpt: Vasudeva said, 'I behold Karna, O son of Kunti... I do not, however, O sinless one, regard the time to have come, O mighty-armed one, for thee to encounter the Suta's son in battle. The blazing dart... given him by Vasava, is still with him... Let the mighty Ghatotkacha proceed against the son of Radha.' ... Then he of Dasarha's race, addressed Hidimva's son... 'Slay Karna in battle, at this dead of night, aided by thy illusions.'

events.working_title: Krishna Directs Ghatotkacha to Slay Alayudha
events.one_line_summary: When Bhima is hard-pressed by the Rakshasa Alayudha, Krishna tells Ghatotkacha to abandon Karna for the moment and first slay Alayudha.

sources.source_excerpt: Vasudeva, approaching Ghatotkacha, said unto him these words, 'Behold, O mighty-armed one, Bhima is violently assailed by the Rakshasa in battle... Abandoning Karna for the present, quickly slay Alayudha, O mighty armed one! Thou can afterwards slay Karna.' Hearing these words of him of Vrishni's race, the valiant Ghatotkacha, abandoning Karna, encountered Alayudha...

events.working_title: Krishna Rejoices at Ghatotkacha's Fall
events.one_line_summary: While the Pandavas mourn Ghatotkacha, Krishna dances and shouts for joy, then reveals the cause: Karna's infallible dart is now spent and Karna is mortal.

sources.source_excerpt: Only Vasudeva filled with transports of delight, began to utter leonine shouts, grieving the Pandavas... Tying the steeds and uttering loud roars, he began to dance in a transport of joy, like a tree shaken by a tempest... Vasudeva said, 'Great is the joy I feel. Listen to me, Dhananjaya!... know, O Dhananjaya, that Karna, his dart being baffled through Ghatotkacha, is already slain in battle.'

events.working_title: Krishna Recounts His Slaying of Enemy Kings
events.one_line_summary: Krishna explains to Arjuna that, for the Pandavas' good, he contrived the deaths of Jarasandha, Ekalavya, Sisupala and Ghatotkacha himself.

sources.source_excerpt: Vasudeva said, 'If Jarasandha, and the ruler of the Chedis, and the mighty son of the Nishada king, had not been slain, they would have become terrible... For thy good, the Nishada's son also... was, by an act of guile, deprived of his thumb by Drona... For thy good, he was slain by me on the field of battle. Endued with great prowess, the ruler of the Chedis was slain by me before thy eyes.'

events.working_title: Krishna Explains His Protection of Arjuna
events.one_line_summary: Krishna tells Satyaki how he always shielded Arjuna from Karna's dart, stupefying Karna so the weapon was never hurled at Partha.

sources.source_excerpt: Vasudeva said, '...I, however, O foremost of warriors, always used to stupefy the son of Radha. It was for this that he did not hurl the dart at Pandu's son... I do not regard my sire, my mother, yourselves, my brothers, ay, my very life, so worthy of protection as Vibhatsu in battle... Beholding Dhananjaya, therefore, like one returned from the dead, these transports of delight, O Yuyudhana, have been mine.'

events.working_title: Krishna Consoles the Grieving Yudhishthira
events.one_line_summary: When Yudhishthira is overwhelmed by grief at Ghatotkacha's death, Krishna urges him to rise and fight rather than sink into despondency.

sources.source_excerpt: Beholding him so afflicted, Krishna said these words, 'O son of Kunti, let not such grief be thine. Such cheerlessness does not become thee, O chief of the Bharatas, as it does an ordinary person. Rise, O king, and fight. Bear the heavy burden, O lord! If cheerlessness overtakes thee, our victory becomes uncertain.'

events.working_title: Krishna Devises the Ashvatthama Stratagem
events.one_line_summary: Seeing Drona unbeatable in battle, Krishna counsels the Pandavas to abandon fair means and tell Drona that his son Ashvatthama is slain, so he will lay down his arms.

sources.source_excerpt: Kesava, endued with great intelligence and devoted to their welfare, addressed Arjuna and said, 'This foremost of all bowmen is incapable of being ever vanquished by force in battle, by the very gods with Vasava at their head. When, however, he lays aside his weapons, he becomes capable of being slain on the field even by human beings. Casting aside virtue, ye sons of Pandu, adopt now some contrivance for gaining the victory... Upon the fall of (his son) Aswatthaman he will cease to fight, I think. Let some man, therefore, tell him that Aswatthaman hath been slain in battle.'

events.working_title: Krishna Urges Yudhishthira to Speak the Untruth
events.one_line_summary: As Drona is about to annihilate the Pandava army, Krishna presses the truth-loving Yudhishthira to tell the half-truth that Ashvatthama is dead.

sources.source_excerpt: Meanwhile, O monarch, Govinda, knowing that Drona... was capable of sweeping all the Pandavas off the face of the earth, became much distressed. Addressing Yudhishthira he said, 'If Drona fighteth, filled with rage, for even half-a-day, I tell thee truly, thy army will then be annihilated. Save us, then, from Drona. Under such circumstances, falsehood is better than truth. By telling an untruth for saving a life, one is not touched by sin. There is no sin in untruth spoken unto women, or in marriages, or for saving a king, or for rescuing a Brahmana.'

events.working_title: Krishna Points Out Karna's Rampage and Urges Arjuna
events.one_line_summary: Krishna, as Arjuna's charioteer, shows Arjuna how Yudhishthira is being pursued and how Karna is ravaging the Pandava army, urging him to advance and slay Karna.

sources.source_excerpt: Meanwhile Krishna, pointing out king Yudhishthira the just, unto Kunti's son Partha, addressed him in these words: 'Yonder, O son of Pandu, your brother (Yudhishthira) is being pursued by many mighty and great bowmen... Righteously setting thy heart on battle, advance against that leader of car-warriors.'

events.working_title: Krishna Advises Arjuna to See the Wounded King First
events.one_line_summary: Krishna tells Arjuna that Yudhishthira has been deeply wounded by Karna and advises him to first see and comfort the king before slaying Karna.

sources.source_excerpt: Thus addressed by Partha, Krishna replied unto that foremost of intelligent men... 'The royal son of Kunti hath been deeply wounded and mangled by Karna. Having seen him first and comforted him, thou wilt then, O Partha, slay Karna.'

events.working_title: Krishna Drives Arjuna to Yudhishthira's Side
events.one_line_summary: Krishna drives the chariot at great speed to the wounded Yudhishthira, and the two Krishnas alight and worship the king's feet.

sources.source_excerpt: Then Hrishikesha proceeded with very great speed to the spot where king Yudhishthira was... Then those two foremost of men, (Krishna and Arjuna), proceeding on their car, approached the king who was lying alone on his bed. Both of them, alighting from that car, worshipped the feet of king Yudhishthira the just.

events.working_title: Krishna Offers Sudarsana to Slay Karna
events.one_line_summary: Seeing Karna baffle Arjuna's weapons, Krishna rebukes Arjuna's slackness and offers him the razor-edged Sudarsana discus to strike off Karna's head.

sources.source_excerpt: Then Vasudeva, beholding Partha's shafts baffled by Karna, said unto the former, 'What is this, O diadem-decked Arjuna, that Karna should succeed in crushing thy weapons today... Putting forth thy might, strike off the head of that foe of thine with this Sudarsana, of edge keen as a razor, that I give unto thee, like Sakra striking off the head of his foe Namuci, with the thunderbolt.'

events.working_title: Krishna Sinks the Chariot to Save Arjuna
events.one_line_summary: When Karna looses the snake-arrow Aswasena at Arjuna's head, Krishna presses the chariot down into the earth with his feet so that the arrow only sweeps off Arjuna's diadem.

sources.source_excerpt: Beholding that shaft blazing in the welkin, the slayer of Kamsa, Madhava, with great speed and the greatest ease, pressed down with his feet that excellent car, causing it to sink about a cubit deep. At this, the steeds, white as the rays of the moon... bending their knees, laid themselves down on the ground.

events.working_title: Krishna Identifies the Snake Aswasena
events.one_line_summary: Krishna names the attacking snake as Aswasena, whose mother Arjuna slew at Khandava, bids Arjuna slay it, and after Arjuna cuts it down raises the sunken chariot with his arms.

sources.source_excerpt: Krishna replied, 'Whilst thou, armed with bow, wert engaged at Khandava in gratifying the god Agni, this snake was then in the sky, his body ensconced within his mother's... Remembering that act of hostility done by thee, he cometh towards thee today for thy destruction.' ... After that snake had been cut off by Arjuna, the lord Keshava himself... raised up with his arms that car from the earth.

events.working_title: Krishna Urges Arjuna to Slay the Distressed Karna
events.one_line_summary: When Arjuna hesitates to strike the stupefied Karna, Krishna urges him not to spare a fallen foe; Karna's chariot-wheel then sinks into the earth and he appeals to Arjuna's righteousness for a moment's respite.

sources.source_excerpt: The younger brother of Indra then, with great excitement, addressed him, saying, 'Why, O son of Pandu, dost thou become so forgetful? They that are truly wise never spare their foes, however weak, even for a moment... Slay him, therefore, like Indra slaying the Asura Namuci.'

events.working_title: The Pandavas Charge Krishna with the Peace Mission
events.one_line_summary: Before his departure for Hastinapura, Bhima, Arjuna and Nakula each address Krishna, urging him to seek peace with the Kauravas and entrusting their cause to him.

sources.source_excerpt: O Krishna, strive thou, therefore, to bring about peace with the foe. Thou, O hero, art the foremost of all friends of both the Pandavas and the Kurus... As soon as thou goest thither, it will be accomplished.

events.working_title: Karna Worships Krishna and Takes His Leave
events.one_line_summary: On the road from Hastinapura, Karna worships Krishna and recounts omens and visions foretelling the Kauravas' defeat; Krishna replies that the destruction of the earth is at hand, and the two part.

sources.source_excerpt: Hearing these beneficial and auspicious words of Kesava, Karna worshipped Krishna, the slayer of Madhu... 'Indeed, the destruction of the earth is at hand when my words, O Karna, do not become acceptable to thy heart...' Having spoken these words, Karna closely pressed Madhava to his bosom. Dismissed by Kesava, he then descended from the car.

events.variant_notes: cf. mb_b_031.

events.working_title: Krishna Returns to Upaplavya and Reports the Failure of the Peace Mission
events.one_line_summary: Krishna returns from Hastinapura and reports to the Pandavas that Duryodhana rejected his true and beneficial words in the assembly.

sources.source_excerpt: Coming back to Upaplavya from Hastinapura, that chastiser of foes, Kesava, represented unto the Pandavas all that had happened... Vasudeva said, 'Having gone to Nagapura, I addressed Dhritarashtra's son in the assembly such words as were true, reasonable, and beneficial. That wicked minded fellow did not, however, accept them.'

events.working_title: Krishna Names Dhrishtadyumna Commander of the Pandava Army
events.one_line_summary: When Yudhishthira asks who should lead the seven Akshauhinis, Krishna approves the candidates and names Dhrishtadyumna as the commander-in-chief.

sources.source_excerpt: the lotus-eyed Krishna said, eyeing Dhananjaya, the while, 'O king, I fully approve of all those powerful warriors whom ye have named for becoming the leaders of thy troops... As regards our leader, I would name that chastiser of foes, Dhrishtadyumna.'

events.working_title: Krishna Declares That War Is Now Inevitable
events.one_line_summary: Pressed by Yudhishthira for guidance, Krishna answers that Duryodhana bears no good will and that, since the Pandavas will not abandon their property, war must now take place.

sources.source_excerpt: Krishna replied, in a voice deep as that of the clouds or cymbals, saying, '...That wicked-souled wight beareth no good will towards thee... As regards ourselves, we do not desire to make peace with the Kauravas by abandoning our property. War, therefore, is that which should now take place.'

events.working_title: Krishna Is Chosen as Arjuna's Charioteer
events.one_line_summary: As the Pandavas marshal their army for Kurukshetra, Krishna is chosen as Arjuna's guide and the driver of his steeds.

sources.source_excerpt: And handsome Janardana endued with great intelligence, he who was the younger brother of Sankarshana, was chosen as the guide of Arjuna and the driver of his steeds.

events.working_title: Balarama Refuses to Take Sides and Departs on Pilgrimage
events.one_line_summary: Balarama, unwilling to fight against either the Pandavas or Duryodhana, declares he follows Krishna's cause but departs to the Saraswati tirthas rather than watch the Kauravas' destruction.

sources.source_excerpt: As regards myself, I dare not cast my eyes on the world without Krishna (on my side). It is for this that I follow whatever Krishna seeketh to achieve... I shall now repair to the tirtha of the Saraswati for ablutions, for I shall not be able to behold with indifference the destruction of the Kauravas.

events.working_title: Krishna Consoles Yudhishthira After the First Day's Battle
events.one_line_summary: Distraught at Bhishma's slaughter of his army, Yudhishthira speaks of retiring to the woods; Krishna consoles him and points to Sikhandin as Bhishma's destined slayer.

sources.source_excerpt: Beholding the son of Pandu stricken with grief and deprived of his senses by sorrow, Govinda then gladdening all the Pandavas said, 'Do not grieve, O chief of the Bharatas... This Sikhandin, O thou of mighty arms, who is certainly the slayer of Bhishma.'

events.working_title: Krishna Drives Arjuna's Chariot Against Bhishma
events.one_line_summary: At Arjuna's bidding, Krishna drives the chariot straight toward Bhishma; in the ensuing duel Bhishma strikes Krishna himself between the breasts with three arrows.

sources.source_excerpt: Unto him Vasudeva then said, 'Be careful, O Dhananjaya, for I will soon take thee, O hero, towards the grandsire's car.' Having said this, O king, Saurin took that car... before the car of Bhishma... Then, O king, Bhishma, that foremost of smiters, struck Vasudeva between his two breasts with three arrows.

events.working_title: Krishna Seizes His Discus and Charges Bhishma
events.one_line_summary: Unable to bear Bhishma's slaughter of the Pandava army, Krishna abandons the chariot reins, leaps down with the discus Sudarshana, and rushes impetuously toward Bhishma to slay him.

sources.source_excerpt: Vasudeva's son, abandoning (the reins of) the steeds, jumped down from the car, whirling with his (right) arm his discus of beautiful nave with edge sharp as a razor, effulgent as the sun... the high-souled Krishna rushed impetuously towards Bhishma... like a lion from desire of slaying upon a prince of elephants blinded with fury.

events.working_title: Arjuna Restrains Krishna, Who Relents and Returns to the Chariot
events.one_line_summary: Arjuna seizes the enraged Krishna and stops him at the tenth step, vowing not to withdraw from the fight; Krishna is gratified, returns to the chariot, and sounds the Panchajanya.

sources.source_excerpt: jumping down from his car, Partha, himself of massive and long arms, quickly ran on foot after that chief of Yadu's race... and seized him by his two hands... succeeded, O king, in stopping him with difficulty at the tenth step... 'Quell this wrath of thine. Thou art the refuge of the Pandavas, O Kesava. I swear... I will not withdraw from the acts to which I have pledged myself.' Hearing that promise and oath of his, Janardana became gratified.

events.working_title: The Pilgrimage to Samanta-panchaka
events.one_line_summary: On the occasion of a solar eclipse, the Yadavas journey to Samanta-panchaka to bathe and give gifts, and there a vast reunion of kings and kinsfolk takes place.

sources.source_excerpt: A great solar eclipse occurs, and the Yadavas, together with Vasudeva, Akrura and others, journey to Samanta-panchaka, the field where Rama had once made lakes of the kings' blood, to bathe and give cows and gifts. There they meet the kings of many realms and their own long-separated kin, and embrace one another with tears of joy. (rendered from Sanskrit, verse 1-15)

events.working_title: Reunion with Nanda and Yashoda
events.one_line_summary: Nanda and the cowherds arrive, and Krishna, Balarama, Yashoda, Devaki and Rohini embrace one another, recalling the old days in Gokula.

sources.source_excerpt: Nanda arrives with the cowherds to see Krishna, and the Vrishnis embrace him as if life itself had returned. Krishna and Balarama bow to their parents and, speechless with love, embrace them; Yashoda takes her two sons on her lap, and Devaki and Rohini, remembering the friendship of old, embrace Yashoda and speak of the love shown to the boys in Gokula. (rendered from Sanskrit, verse 30-37)

events.working_title: Krishna's Counsel to the Gopis
events.one_line_summary: Krishna meets the gopis, who have long pined for him, embraces them, and teaches them that all beings abide in him, and that their love for him grants immortality.

sources.source_excerpt: The gopis, seeing Krishna after so long, embrace him in their hearts and attain that state which even the ever-yoked cannot easily gain. Krishna asks whether they remember his friendship, and teaches them that as the wind scatters clouds, so the Lord unites and separates beings, and that devotion to him grants immortality — by which instruction the gopis, their bondage dissolved, attained him. (rendered from Sanskrit, verse 38-47)

events.working_title: Vasudeva's Sacrifice
events.one_line_summary: The sages, pleased with Vasudeva's question, initiate him and he performs a great sacrifice at Samanta-panchaka, with his sons and the Yadavas attending.

sources.source_excerpt: Vasudeva, instructed by the sages, chooses them as his priests, and they initiate him and perform sacrifices at that holy field. Krishna and Balarama shine there among their kinsmen and sons, and after the rites Vasudeva gives rich gifts of cows, land and maidens to the priests, completing the sacrifice with the avabhritha bath. (rendered from Sanskrit, verse 42-55)

events.working_title: Nanda's Farewell
events.one_line_summary: Vasudeva, overcome with love, laments that riches blinded him to old friends, and Nanda, honored by the Yadavas with rich gifts, departs for Mathura with the cowherds.

sources.source_excerpt: Vasudeva, weeping as he recalls the friendship, tells Nanda that the snare called affection is hard to cast off, and that blinded by royal splendor he neglected his old friend. Nanda stays three months, honored by the Yadavas, and then, laden with rich gifts from Vasudeva, Ugrasena, Krishna and Uddhava, departs with the cowherds, his heart fixed on Krishna's lotus feet. (rendered from Sanskrit, verse 58-69)

events.working_title: Devaki Asks for Her Slain Sons
events.one_line_summary: Devaki, remembering the six sons Kamsa killed, tearfully asks Krishna and Balarama to bring back her dead children.

sources.source_excerpt: Hearing of how Krishna and Balarama had brought back their guru's son, Devaki, remembering the sons slaughtered by Kamsa, tearfully asks them to grant her wish to see her slain children restored. She recalls that they had once fetched their guru's dead son as a fee, and entreats them to bring back the sons slain by the Bhoja king. (rendered from Sanskrit, verse 26-32)

events.working_title: Krishna and Balarama Visit Bali in Sutala
events.one_line_summary: Krishna and Balarama descend to Sutala, where Bali, the daitya king, receives them with great devotion, and Krishna reveals the true origin of Devaki's six sons.

sources.source_excerpt: Entering Sutala by their yoga-maya, Krishna and Balarama are received by the daitya king Bali, who rises, bows, and washes their feet with his kin. Krishna then reveals that the six sons were once the six sons of Marichi, who laughed at Brahma and were cursed to be born as demons — the very children Kamsa killed, who now dwell nearby awaiting release. (rendered from Sanskrit, verse 33-51)

events.working_title: The Six Sons Restored to Devaki
events.one_line_summary: Krishna and Balarama bring the six sons back from Sutala; Devaki nurses them with her milk, and, released from the curse, they bow and ascend to the gods' abode.

sources.source_excerpt: Taking the six sons, Krishna and Balarama return to Dwaraka and give them to their mother, and Devaki, her breasts flowing with milk, nurses and embraces them. Having drunk her milk, they bow to Krishna, Devaki, Vasudeva and Balarama, and before the eyes of all beings ascend to the abode of the gods. (rendered from Sanskrit, verse 51-56)

events.working_title: Krishna Visits Shrutadeva and Bahulashva
events.one_line_summary: Krishna, to please both the sage Shrutadeva and King Bahulashva of Mithila, visits both their homes simultaneously, unseen by each other.

sources.source_excerpt: Krishna travels to Mithila with the sages, and both the brahmana Shrutadeva and King Bahulashva, each thinking Krishna has come to his own house, invite him and the sages. To please both devotees, Krishna enters both homes at once, unseen by either, and each worships him with overflowing devotion. (rendered from Sanskrit, verse 23-36)

events.working_title: Krishna's Sons and the Yadu Lineage
events.one_line_summary: The text enumerates Krishna's sixteen thousand wives and his many sons — Pradyumna, Aniruddha and others — and traces the line through Vajra, the sole Yadu survivor of the coming internecine war.

sources.source_excerpt: Krishna has sixteen thousand and more than a hundred queens, and on each he begets ten sons; among the foremost are Pradyumna, Aniruddha, Samba and others. Pradyumna's grandson through Aniruddha is Vajra, who alone would survive the destruction by the mace, and the Yadava line is declared too vast to count. (rendered from Sanskrit, verse 28-45)

events.working_title: Kunti's Farewell Hymn to Krishna
events.one_line_summary: As Krishna prepares to leave Hastinapura for Dwaraka, Queen Kunti offers a parting eulogy recalling how he saved her family from poison, fire, exile and weapons, and asks only that his remembrance ever bind her; Krishna smiles and grants her prayer.

sources.source_excerpt: Freed from the brahma weapon, Kunti addressed Krishna as he turned to depart: 'I bow to you, the primal Person... You freed Devaki and me, with my sons, again and again from danger — from poison, from the great fire, from the cruel assembly, from the hardships of forest exile, from the weapons of great chariot-warriors.' And the Lord, whose every glory she had praised, smiled gently. (rendered from Sanskrit, verses 16-17, 22, 43)

events.working_title: Krishna Departs Hastinapura for Dwaraka
events.one_line_summary: After restoring Yudhishthira to the throne and staying some months to comfort his relatives, Krishna takes leave of the grieving Pandavas and women of Hastinapura and sets out for Dwaraka, journeying through many kingdoms.

sources.source_excerpt: Having stayed in Hastinapura some months to gladden his friends and please his sister, Hari took his leave, embraced and bowed to all, and mounted his chariot; Subhadra, Draupadi, Kunti, Gandhari, Dhritarashtra and the others could not bear the separation, their eyes fixed on him as he departed. (rendered from Sanskrit, verses 6-12)

events.working_title: Krishna's Homecoming to Dwaraka
events.one_line_summary: Krishna reaches his own prosperous realm of Anarta, sounds his conch, and is welcomed by the joyful citizens, his father Vasudeva, Balarama, Ugrasena and his queens, who receive him with offerings and embrace.

sources.source_excerpt: Approaching his own prosperous land of Anarta, Krishna blew his conch to dispel his people's sorrow; hearing it, the citizens rushed to see their lord. Vasudeva, Akrura, Ugrasena and the wondrous Rama, with Pradyumna and others, came forth on chariots to meet him; entering his father's house, Krishna bowed to his seven mothers led by Devaki, who lifted him to their laps and bathed him with tears of joy. (rendered from Sanskrit, verses 1-2, 16-18, 28-29)

events.working_title: Arjuna Brings News of the Yadava End
events.one_line_summary: Arjuna returns from Dwaraka broken and weeping and tells Yudhishthira how the Yadavas, deluded by a brahmin's curse and drunk on wine, slew one another with their fists, and how Krishna then departed the earth, after which the Kali age set in.

sources.source_excerpt: Arjuna, his heart hollowed by grief, tells the king: 'In the city of our friends, the Yadavas, deluded by the curse of the brahmins, drinking the madira wine and beside themselves, slew one another with their bare fists; but four or five were left.' And Suta adds: when Mukunda abandoned this earth, in that very moment the Kali age, the cause of all evil for the unawakened, entered. (rendered from Sanskrit, verses 21-22, 35)

events.variant_notes: Arjuna's report of the Yadava end; cf. bpc1_030.

events.working_title: Brahma and the Gods Urge Krishna to Return to His Abode
events.one_line_summary: After one hundred and twenty-five years, Brahma and the assembled gods come to Dwaraka, praise Krishna, and remind him that the earth's burden is lifted and his clan is nearly consumed by the curse, asking him to return to his own abode.

sources.source_excerpt: Brahma said: 'A hundred and twenty-five years have passed since you descended in the Yadu line. Your work for the gods is all but done, and this clan is nearly destroyed by the brahmins' curse. If you think fit, return to your supreme abode.' Krishna answered that the earth's burden was indeed lifted and he would go at the end of the curse. (rendered from Sanskrit, verses 24-30)

events.variant_notes: Prefigures the departure; cf. bpc1_029.

events.working_title: Uddhava Begs Krishna Not to Leave Him Behind
events.one_line_summary: Seeing the fearful omens in Dwaraka and Krishna's intention to depart, Uddhava falls at his feet and pleads that he cannot bear to be separated even for a moment and begs to be taken along; Krishna, granting his wish, begins to instruct him.

sources.source_excerpt: Uddhava said: 'Lord, even for half a moment I cannot bear to leave your lotus feet; carry me also to your abode.' Krishna, addressed by his devoted servant, answered: 'What you have said is exactly my own intent; Brahma, Shiva and the world-guardians long for my return to heaven.' (rendered from Sanskrit, verses 41-42, 49-50)

events.working_title: Krishna's Last Message to Daruka
events.one_line_summary: Krishna consoles the hunter, granting him heaven, and when his charioteer Daruka weeps at his feet, sends him to Dwaraka with the final message: the Yadavas are destroyed, Balarama is gone, and the sea will swallow Dwaraka, so let the people follow Arjuna to Indraprastha.

sources.source_excerpt: Krishna said to Jara: 'Fear not; rise. This was my own doing. Go, with my leave, to the abode of the virtuous.' And to his charioteer he said: 'Go to Dwaraka and tell my kinsmen of the destruction and of Balarama's departure and of my state. The sea will soon flood the city I have left; let all of you, with Arjuna's help, go to Indraprastha.' (rendered from Sanskrit, verses 38-39, 45-47)

events.variant_notes: cf. mb_d_019; follows the shooting (bpc1_027).

events.working_title: Krishna's Final Instruction to Uddhava
events.one_line_summary: Uddhava recalls how, as the Yadavas destroyed themselves, Krishna sat at the foot of an ashvattha tree and, finding Uddhava there, granted him the ancient teaching and the supreme state, commanding him to go to Badari.
locations: at the foot of an ashvattha tree

sources.source_excerpt: Uddhava said: 'The Lord, seeing that course of his own maya, sipped the Sarasvati and sat at the foot of a tree; he said to me, go to Badari. Yet, unable to leave his feet, I followed; and he, finding me there, told me: I know your heart's desire; I grant you what is hard for others to attain. And he taught me the supreme state.' (rendered from Sanskrit, verses 2-10, 18)

events.variant_notes: The final teaching; cf. Uddhava's departure cluster (bpc1_024).

events.working_title: Krishna Substitutes an Iron Statue for Bhima
events.one_line_summary: Sensing Dhritarashtra's murderous intent, Krishna drags away the real Bhima and substitutes an iron statue, which the blind king crushes in his embrace; Krishna then reveals the trick and consoles him.

sources.source_excerpt: Ascertaining the evil intentions cherished by him towards Bhima, Krishna, dragging away the real Bhima, presented an iron statue of the second son of Pandu to the old king... Understanding that he was no longer under the influence of wrath... Vasudeva, that foremost of men, said these words, 'Do not grieve, O Dhritarashtra, for thou hast not slain Bhimasena! That is an iron statue, O king, which has been broken by thee!'

events.working_title: Krishna Counsels Dhritarashtra to Govern His Wrath
events.one_line_summary: Krishna admonishes Dhritarashtra that his sorrow is his own fault and urges him to restrain his wrath; the king is pacified and embraces and blesses the Pandavas.

sources.source_excerpt: 'Why then dost thou cherish such wrath when all that has overtaken thee is the result of thy own fault? ... Recollecting thy own faults, govern thy wrath now.' ... 'Now, however, I am free from wrath and fever. I desire eagerly, O Madhava, to embrace that hero, the second son of Pandu.'

events.working_title: Gandhari Curses Krishna; He Accepts with a Smile
events.one_line_summary: Grieving her sons, Gandhari curses Krishna that in the thirty-sixth year he will see his own kinsmen slain and himself perish in the wilderness; Krishna, smiling, accepts that only the Vrishnis themselves can destroy the Vrishnis.

sources.source_excerpt: Since thou wert indifferent to the Kurus and the Pandavas whilst they slew each other, therefore, O Govinda, thou shalt be the slayer of thy own kinsmen! In the thirty-sixth year from this... thou shalt... perish by disgusting means in the wilderness. Hearing these words, the high-souled Vasudeva... said unto her these words, with a faint smile, 'There is none in the world, save myself, that is capable of exterminating the Vrishnis... In uttering this curse, O thou of excellent vows, thou hast aided me in the accomplishment of that task.'

events.variant_notes: Gandhari's curse; cf. mb_d_013 (the sages' curse).

events.working_title: Krishna Rebukes Gandhari
events.one_line_summary: Krishna tells Gandhari to arise and not grieve, declaring the carnage came through her own fault and Duryodhana's wickedness, not through him.

sources.source_excerpt: 'Arise, arise, O Gandhari, do not set thy heart on grief! Through thy fault, this vast carnage has taken place! Thy son Duryodhana was wicked-souled, envious, and exceedingly arrogant... Why dost thou wish to ascribe thy own faults to me?'

events.working_title: Arjuna Asks Krishna to Repeat the Gita; Krishna Offers the Anugita
events.one_line_summary: After the war, Arjuna confesses he has forgotten the Gita's teaching and asks Krishna to repeat it; Krishna says he cannot recite it again in detail and instead narrates an old history (the Anugita).

sources.source_excerpt: Arjuna... addressed his companion, saying, '...What thy holy self said unto me at that time, O Kesava, through affection, has all been forgotten by me, O chief of men, in consequence of the fickleness of my mind.' ... Vasudeva said, '...It is impossible for me, O Dhananjaya, to repeat, in detail, all that I said on that occasion... I shalt now, however, recite to thee an old history upon the same topic.'

events.working_title: Samva Brings Forth the Iron Bolt; Wine Is Prohibited
events.one_line_summary: The next day Samva brings forth the iron bolt; king Ugrasena has it ground to powder and cast into the sea, and at the command of Krishna, Rama and others a prohibition on wine is proclaimed throughout Dwaraka.

sources.source_excerpt: When the next day came, Samva actually brought forth an iron bolt through which all the individuals in the race of the Vrishnis and the Andhakas became consumed into ashes... In great distress of mind, the king (Ugrasena) caused that iron bolt to be reduced into fine powder... it was, again, proclaimed throughout the city that from that day, among all the Vrishnis and the Andhakas no one should manufacture wines and intoxicating spirits of any kind.

events.variant_notes: cf. mb_d_013.

events.working_title: Krishna Sends Daruka for Arjuna; Vabhru Is Slain
events.one_line_summary: Krishna sends Daruka to summon Arjuna and commands Vabhru to protect the women; Vabhru, still dazed with wine, is slain by the iron bolt that springs from a hunter's mallet.

sources.source_excerpt: Krishna commanded Daruka, saying, 'Going to the Kurus, inform Partha of this great slaughter of the Yadus. Let Arjuna come here quickly...' ... Vabhru... as soon as he had proceeded to a distance, the iron-bolt, attaching itself to a mallet in the hands of a hunter, suddenly sprang of itself upon that solitary survivor of the Yadava race and slew him.

events.variant_notes: cf. bpc1_028 (Daruka's errand).

events.working_title: Krishna Entrusts the Women to Vasudeva
events.one_line_summary: Krishna returns to Dwaraka, tells his father Vasudeva to protect the women until Arjuna comes, touches his father's feet, and retraces his steps to comfort the wailing ladies.

sources.source_excerpt: Entering the city of Dwaravati, Janardana said these words unto his father, 'Do thou protect all the ladies of our house, till Dhananjaya comes...' Having said these words, Krishna touched the feet of his father with his head, and quickly left his presence. Then a loud wail of sorrow arose from the ladies... Keshava retraced his foot-steps and said unto them, 'Arjuna will come here. That foremost of men will relieve you of your grief.'

events.working_title: The Abhiras Rob Arjuna
events.one_line_summary: Leading Krishna's widowed wives and wealth from Dwaraka, Arjuna is set upon by Abhira robbers; his bow Gandiva goes slack, his weapons fail, and the thieves carry off the women and treasure.

sources.source_excerpt: Thereupon Arjuna began to brace his heavenly bow Gándíva... but it was in vain; for, in spite of all his efforts to tighten it, it continued flaccid... the barbarians, in the sight of Arjuna, carried off all the women of the Vrishńi and Andhaka tribes.

events.variant_notes: Aftermath of the submergence; cf. bpc1_030.

events.working_title: Vyasa Consoles Arjuna and Parikshit Is Enthroned
events.one_line_summary: Vyasa tells Arjuna that Krishna's departure was the will of time and recounts Ashtavakra's curse on the Apsarasas; Arjuna installs Vajra in Mathura, and the Pandavas place Parikshit on the throne.

sources.source_excerpt: Vyása replied to Arjuna, and said, "Think no more, my son, of your disgrace... Know that time subjects all beings to similar vicissitude." ...the sons of Páńd́u placed Paríkshit on the throne, and went to the forest.

events.variant_notes: cf. vp5_038_01 (Dwaraka sinks).

events.working_title: Earth, Oppressed by Demon-Kings, Seeks Brahma
events.one_line_summary: The Earth, burdened by arrogant demon kings, takes the form of a weeping cow and appeals to Brahma for relief.

sources.source_excerpt: The Earth, crushed by the weight of countless demon kings, assumes the form of a cow, tearful and exhausted, and laments her misery before Brahma. (rendered from Sanskrit, verse 16-17)

events.working_title: Vishnu Promises to Descend into the House of Vasudeva
events.one_line_summary: Brahma and the gods carry the Earth's plea to Vishnu on the milk ocean; a divine voice declares Vishnu will be born in Vasudeva's house and that the gods should descend as helpers.

sources.source_excerpt: Brahma, bearing the Earth, goes with the gods to the shore of the milk ocean; a voice from the sky declares that the Supreme Lord himself will be born in Vasudeva's home, and the gods should descend in part to aid him. (rendered from Sanskrit, verse 18-24)

events.working_title: Narada Curses Nalakuvara and Manigriva
events.one_line_summary: Drunk and naked in a river with celestial women, Kubera's sons insult Narada, who curses them to become twin arjuna trees until Krishna's touch frees them.

sources.source_excerpt: Intoxicated with wine, the two sons of Kubera sport naked with women in the Ganga; the sage Narada, to cure their pride, curses them to stand as twin arjuna trees, promising release at the touch of Vasudeva. (rendered from Sanskrit, verse 1-22)

events.working_title: Vrikasura's Lethal Boon from Shiva
events.one_line_summary: The asura Vrikasura wins from Shiva the boon that whoever's head he touches will die, then tries to test it on Shiva himself, who flees in terror to Vaikuntha.

sources.source_excerpt: The asura Vrikasura, son of Shakuni, performs terrible penance and wins from the compassionate Shiva the boon that whomever he touches on the head shall die. To test it, he tries to place his hand on Shiva's own head, and the terrified Shiva, pursued by the asura, flees to the ends of the earth and heavens and finally takes refuge in Vaikuntha. (rendered from Sanskrit, verse 12-27)

events.variant_notes: cf. bp10d_048 (Vishnu's rescue of Shiva).

events.working_title: Vishnu Saves Shiva from Vrikasura
events.one_line_summary: Vishnu, appearing as a young brahmachari, tricks Vrikasura into touching his own head, and the asura destroys himself, freeing Shiva.

sources.source_excerpt: Vishnu, taking the form of a radiant young brahmachari, receives the exhausted Vrikasura and, feigning disbelief in Shiva's boon, tells him to test it by placing his hand on his own head. The bewildered asura does so and instantly splits his own skull and dies, while the gods shower flowers and the freed Shiva praises Vishnu, the deliverer of those who offend the great. (rendered from Sanskrit, verse 28-38)

events.working_title: Bhrigu Tests the Three Gods
events.one_line_summary: Sent by the sages to test who is greatest, Bhrigu finds Brahma and Shiva angered, but Vishnu, far from being offended, apologizes and serves him, proving Vishnu supreme.

sources.source_excerpt: To settle which of the three gods is greatest, the sages send Bhrigu; Brahma grows angry at Bhrigu's disrespect but restrains himself, and Shiva raises his trident to slay him till the goddess intervenes. Vishnu, however, on being kicked in the chest by Bhrigu, rises and apologizes, asking the sage to forgive him — and Bhrigu, moved, declares Vishnu alone the abode of peace and fearlessness. (rendered from Sanskrit, verse 1-18)

events.working_title: Yadu Meets the Wandering Avadhuta
events.one_line_summary: King Yadu meets a serene, fearless brahmin avadhuta and, astonished at his freedom, asks how he attained such wisdom; the avadhuta answers that he has twenty-four gurus from whom he drew his understanding.

sources.source_excerpt: Yadu asked the wandering brahmin: 'You act like a child, a madman, a ghost, and yet you are a sage; how did you gain such wisdom?' The brahmin answered: 'I have many gurus, O king — earth, wind, sky, water, fire, moon, sun, the pigeon, the python, the ocean, the moth, the bee, the elephant, the honey-gatherer, the deer, the fish, Pingala, the osprey, the child, the maiden, the arrow-maker, the serpent, the spider and the wasp — twenty-four in all.' (rendered from Sanskrit, verses 26-34)

events.working_title: The Avadhuta's Lessons from the Elements
events.one_line_summary: The avadhuta relates what he learned from the earth, wind, sky, water, fire, moon and sun: forbearance, detachment, unaffectedness, purity, untaintedness, waxing and waning, and the one soul reflected in many bodies.

sources.source_excerpt: The avadhuta said: 'Though trampled by all beings, the wise one does not stray from his path — this I learned from the earth. Moving among the objects of sense, the yogi remains unattached like the wind; pure and sweet like water; untainted by what he consumes, like fire; waxing and waning like the moon; one soul appearing in many bodies, like the sun.' (rendered from Sanskrit, verses 36-50)

events.working_title: The Pigeon and the Hunter's Net
events.one_line_summary: A pigeon so bound to his mate and chicks that when a hunter's net traps his family he casts himself into the same net and perishes with them, teaching Krishna's hearers that clinging to home and family destroys.

sources.source_excerpt: The pigeon, seeing his chicks and his mate caught in the hunter's net, lamented: 'Alas, my poor mind! My home is destroyed; of what use is my life now?' And he too flew into the net, and the cruel hunter took them all. 'Thus the householder who feeds his family like a bird, attached and without peace, comes to ruin.' (rendered from Sanskrit, verses 66-72)

events.working_title: The Python's Contentment and the Ocean's Depth
events.one_line_summary: The avadhuta learns from the python to accept whatever food chance brings without striving, and from the ocean to remain deep, full and unmoved whether rivers pour in or not.

sources.source_excerpt: The avadhuta said: 'The python eats whatever comes by chance, whether fine or foul, much or little, and lies still for days without food if nothing comes. The sage is serene and unfathomable like the ocean, which neither swells when rivers pour in nor dries when they do not.' (rendered from Sanskrit, verses 1-5)

events.working_title: The Moth and the Bee
events.one_line_summary: From the moth, which perishes in the flame, the avadhuta learns that desire for a woman's beauty destroys; from the bee he learns to take only the essence from many flowers without storing anything up.

sources.source_excerpt: The avadhuta said: 'Bewitched by a woman's beauty, the uncontrolled man falls into blinding darkness like the moth into the flame. And the sage gathers the essence from great and small teachings, like the bee from flowers, but stores nothing for tomorrow.' (rendered from Sanskrit, verses 6-9)

events.working_title: The Elephant, the Honey-Gatherer, the Deer and the Fish
events.one_line_summary: The avadhuta learns from the elephant, ensnared by lust for the decoy she-elephant, from the honey-gatherer, whose hoard others enjoy, from the deer, snared while listening to music, and from the fish, hooked through the tongue, how the senses lead one to ruin.

sources.source_excerpt: The avadhuta said: 'The ascetic should not touch a woman even of wood, lest he be bound like the elephant caught by the she-elephant; the wealth painfully hoarded is enjoyed by others, as the honey-gatherer steals the bees' honey; the deer is snared by song; and the fish, allured by the tongue's bait, meets death on the hook.' (rendered from Sanskrit, verses 12-18)

events.working_title: Pingala the Courtesan's Renunciation
events.one_line_summary: The courtesan Pingala, waiting through the night for a client who never comes, is seized with disgust at her own longing, renounces it, and sleeps in peace, teaching that hope is the worst of pains and despair the highest joy.

sources.source_excerpt: Pingala said: 'Look at the extent of my delusion! I sought a lover for gain, when the giver of all joy is ever near. What I sought so wretchedly, let me give up.' Cutting off her hope of a lover, Pingala sat down and slept in peace: 'Hope is the greatest of pains; freedom from hope is the greatest of joys.' (rendered from Sanskrit, verses 30, 42-43)

events.working_title: The Osprey, the Child, the Maiden and the Arrow-Maker
events.one_line_summary: The avadhuta learns from the osprey (letting go of prey seized by stronger birds), the child (freedom from care), the maiden (solitude — she broke her bangles one by one to stop their clinking), and the arrow-maker (one-pointed concentration).

sources.source_excerpt: The avadhuta said: 'A maiden, alone, husking grain, heard her bangles clink and broke them one by one until only one remained, and it was silent — so the sage should dwell alone. And like the arrow-maker so absorbed in straightening his shaft that he did not see the king pass by, the mind should be fixed on one point.' (rendered from Sanskrit, verses 4-12)

events.working_title: The Serpent, the Spider and the Wasp
events.one_line_summary: The avadhuta learns from the serpent (dwelling in another's abandoned hole, homeless), from the spider (who spins the web from himself and withdraws it again), and from the wasp (who becomes what it meditates upon).

sources.source_excerpt: The avadhuta said: 'Building a house brings only sorrow — the serpent enters another's abandoned home and thrives. As the spider sends forth the thread from its own heart, plays with it and draws it back, so the Lord creates, sustains and withdraws the world. And as the wasp, meditating on its captor, becomes like it, so the mind becomes what it dwells upon.' (rendered from Sanskrit, verses 14, 20-22)

events.working_title: The Swan Teaches the Kumaras
events.one_line_summary: Asked by his disciples about the swan form, Krishna recounts how Brahma's sons Sanaka and the others, unable to get an answer from Brahma, were taught by Krishna himself appearing as a swan (hamsa), who resolved their doubt.

sources.source_excerpt: Krishna said: 'The mind-born sons of Brahma asked him the subtle goal of yoga; pondering their question, Brahma meditated on me, and I appeared to them in the form of a swan. They asked who I was, and I answered that if in truth there is no difference in the self, their very question has no ground — know that I alone am, and nothing apart from me.' (rendered from Sanskrit, verses 15-23)

events.working_title: The Miserly Brahmin of Avanti
events.one_line_summary: A wealthy but miserly brahmin of Avanti, spurned by his own relatives and stripped of his wealth, is seized with dispassion, becomes a wandering mendicant, and, enduring the mockery and blows of the crowd, sings the song of the mendicant: the mind alone is the cause of joy and sorrow.

sources.source_excerpt: The brahmin of Avanti, once wealthy, miserly and cruel, saw his wealth taken by relatives and thieves; dispassion arose, and he became a silent, wandering mendicant. Though people seized his staff, mocked and struck him, he sang: 'Neither people, nor gods, nor fate are the cause of my joy and sorrow — it is the mind alone that turns the wheel of existence.' (rendered from Sanskrit, verses 5-11, 41)

events.working_title: Pururava's Lament for Urvashi
events.one_line_summary: King Pururava (Aila), mad with grief when the nymph Urvashi leaves him, pursues her naked and weeping; realizing his delusion, he sings the song of Aila on the futility of attachment to women, and attains peace.

sources.source_excerpt: King Aila sang: 'Alas, what delusion has seized me! A monarch, I became a plaything of a woman; I, who was emperor, followed her like a beast, naked and weeping. What is this foul body of flesh and bone, and what these charms imputed to it? So let no wise man cling to women.' (rendered from Sanskrit, verses 6-21)

events.working_title: Vidura Meets the Grieving Uddhava
events.one_line_summary: On the banks of the Yamuna, Vidura meets Uddhava, who is plunged in grief and remembrance of Krishna's departure, and hears him lament that the Yadavas never recognized the Lord who dwelt among them.

sources.source_excerpt: Uddhava, asked by Vidura, was for a moment silent, sunk in the nectar of Krishna's feet, his limbs thrilling with devotion; then, wiping his eyes, he smiled and said: 'The sun Krishna has set; what good news can I tell in homes bereft of fortune? Wretched is this world, and more so the Yadavas, who dwelt with Hari and knew him not.' (rendered from Sanskrit, verses 3-7)
